name: Allicin (garlic compound)
short: Garlic, not allicin capsules: spinal bleed with paralysis, surgical bleeding, anaphylaxis; skin burns, incl. young children. Allicin, H. pylori trials: side effects not more common (very low quality).
text: This entry covers allicin, a compound from garlic, taken by mouth as capsules; harms reported with garlic itself are given separately and labelled, and do not come from allicin capsules. Allicin by mouth: a 2019 meta-analysis of 8 randomized trials (867 participants) of allicin added to Helicobacter pylori treatment found no significant difference in side effects, but rated the side-effect evidence very low quality because of risk of bias and indirectness. In a randomized trial of 220 people with H. pylori, a regimen containing an allicin soft capsule (described in the abstract as 40 mg of DATS, which it does not define) had an adverse-event rate of 10.9%, against 14.5% with a bismuth regimen (P = 0.418), with both regimens also containing ilaprazole, doxycycline and furazolidone for 14 days, so these rates describe whole regimens; nausea was reported as more frequent with the bismuth regimen (P = 0.030), although the abstract's figures (1.8% vs 8.2%) are given without saying which belongs to which group. In a 12-week pilot study of oral allicin in 20 people with Behcet's disease, some side effects were observed and went away when allicin was stopped; the abstract does not name them. In a 12-week trial included in a Cochrane review, 146 people took a garlic supplement described as containing 180 mg of allicin, or placebo, once daily; adverse effects included rash and odour (the abstract does not say in which group). A further study, whose abstract does not give the route, the form or the number of volunteers (so it may not be of allicin by mouth), reports no side effects in normal volunteers taking allicin daily for 8 weeks. Garlic (not allicin capsules): a review of human data reports garlic breath and body odour as the commonest complaints in trials, and case reports of allergic reactions (including generalised hives, angioedema and anaphylaxis), of altered platelet function and blood clotting with a possible risk of bleeding, and of burns when fresh garlic is applied to the skin, especially under dressings. A review of supplements and bleeding found garlic supplements strongly associated with bleeding during surgery, independent of anticoagulants. Case reports describe anaphylaxis after eating raw garlic, which the authors say could be life-threatening, and an anaphylactic reaction after eating young garlic in a 23-year-old woman who already had pollen and dried-fruit allergy and food-dependent, exercise-induced anaphylaxis; another record, known only by its title, describes garlic-induced severe anaphylaxis in a nonatopic patient (one without a tendency to allergies), and the route cannot be reported. Case reports describe a bleed around the spinal cord (spinal epidural haematoma) causing paralysis of both legs in a person in their nineties with a platelet disorder from excessive garlic eating, who recovered satisfactorily, marked blood in the urine after a minimally invasive urological procedure in a 65-year-old man taking long-term garlic supplements, and a spinal epidural haematoma (from the third to fifth thoracic vertebrae) needing emergency surgery in a 60-year-old woman who had been taking a herbal medicine containing black garlic for 8 weeks (the abstract does not list its other ingredients); she recovered after surgery. Garlic on the skin or in the mouth (a different route): a 46-year-old man had a second-degree chemical burn with large blisters after crushed raw garlic was left on his wrist for 5 hours; the authors note that crushing garlic forms allicin. Severe irritant dermatitis developed on the neck of an infant who wore a fresh garlic necklace for nasal congestion, a 15-month-old child had burns to the feet after raw garlic was applied as a home remedy for fever, two further records known only by their titles describe plantar garlic burns in a 7-month-old infant and chemical burns in children whose warts were treated with garlic, and a 49-year-old man had a burn with local tissue death in his mouth after applying crushed raw garlic for tooth pain. Interactions (garlic): the review says garlic may enhance the effect of anticoagulants such as warfarin and fluindione; in 10 healthy volunteers, garlic supplements lowered blood levels of the HIV medicine saquinavir (area under the curve down 51%). The allicin abstracts give no interaction data. The cited sources give no data on pregnancy.
